title: 22. Interview: Encryption in Transit
summary: Interview Q&A for Encryption in Transit — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Encryption in Transit interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is forward secrecy, and why does TLS 1.3 make it mandatory?
**Answer:** Forward secrecy is the property that compromising the server's long-term private key (e.g., a future breach, a court order, an HSM theft) does not allow decryption of past recorded traffic. It works because every TLS session uses an ephemeral key agreement (ECDHE — Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral): the client and server each generate a fresh key pair for the session, derive the shared session key, then destroy the ephemeral private keys. The session key is never stored and never derivable from the long-term keys — it exists only in RAM during the session. An attacker who recorded all traffic and later steals the server's private key cannot reconstruct the ephemeral keys (they are gone), so the recorded ciphertext is unrecoverable. TLS 1.2 made forward secrecy optional (it allowed static RSA key exchange, where the session key was encrypted to the server's long-term public key — recoverable from a future key compromise). TLS 1.3 dropped static RSA and requires ECDHE for every connection, making forward secrecy universal. This is why nation-state adversaries who record encrypted traffic for later decryption (the "store now, decrypt later" attack) lost significant capability with TLS 1.3.

**Visual:**
```
TLS 1.2 (static RSA, NO forward secrecy):
  session_key = RSA_encrypt(server_pub)  -> recorded traffic + later key theft = decrypt
TLS 1.3 (ECDHE, forward secrecy):
  session_key = ECDHE(client_eph, server_eph)
  ephemeral keys destroyed after session -> future key theft cannot recover
```

### Q2. Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
**Answer:** Each solves a different problem and has different performance characteristics. Asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, ECDHE) is used during the handshake to authenticate the server (via the certificate signature), authenticate the client (in mTLS), and exchange key material (via ECDHE) — but it is slow: RSA operations are ~1000x slower per byte than AES. Symmetric crypto (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) is used for bulk application data because it is fast (~5-10 GB/s per core with AES-NI) and provides both confidentiality and integrity in one operation (authenticated encryption). The pattern is universal in secure protocols: use slow asymmetric crypto once at the start to authenticate and establish a shared secret, then use fast symmetric crypto for everything after. TLS 1.3 reinforces this by separating the handshake (asymmetric, may use RSA or ECDSA for cert signature, ECDHE for key agreement) from the record layer (symmetric, AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). The session key derived from ECDHE is fed into a key schedule that produces separate keys for each direction (client-to-server, server-to-client) and for handshake vs. application data.

**Visual:**
```
handshake (asymmetric, slow but once):
  cert signature: Ed25519/ECDSA  (authenticate server)
  key agreement:  ECDHE          (derive session key)
                |
                v
record layer (symmetric, fast, every byte):
  AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305
  with session key from handshake
```

### Q3. What is the difference between TLS termination at the edge and end-to-end TLS?
**Answer:** Edge termination means TLS is decrypted at the CDN or load balancer (the "edge" of your infrastructure) and traffic flows plaintext from there to the backend servers — over the internal network or a private link. This is simple, lets the LB inspect HTTP headers for routing, and lets the WAF inspect the request body, but it means plaintext crosses the internal network, which is unacceptable for sensitive traffic (PII, payment data, health data) and violates some compliance regimes (PCI-DSS requires encryption until the decryption point, which must be in the cardholder data environment). End-to-end TLS means TLS is established all the way from the client to the application server, with the LB operating in TCP passthrough mode — the LB cannot inspect HTTP headers and cannot do L7 routing or health checks, but the traffic is encrypted end-to-end. The compromise is two-tier TLS: TLS terminates at the LB (for routing and WAF), then a second TLS connection is established from the LB to the backend (for internal encryption) — the internal segment is encrypted even though it crosses the internal network. AWS ALB and most modern LBs support this; it costs a bit more (TLS processing at two layers) and adds ~1-2 ms of latency, but the security gain is worth it for sensitive workloads.

**Visual:**
```
edge termination:
  client --[TLS]--> LB --[plaintext]--> backend   (simple, internal plaintext)
end-to-end:
  client --[TLS]--> LB (TCP passthrough) --[TLS]--> backend   (LB can't route on L7)
two-tier (best of both):
  client --[TLS]--> LB --[TLS]--> backend   (LB routes on L7, internal encrypted)
```

### Q4. What is mutual TLS (mTLS) and when should you use it?
**Answer:** Mutual TLS is TLS where both sides present and validate certificates — the server authenticates the client in addition to the client authenticating the server. In standard one-way TLS (used for public HTTPS), only the server presents a certificate; the client is authenticated at the application layer (cookie, API key, OAuth token) after the TLS session is established. In mTLS, the client also has a certificate (typically issued by an internal CA, often with a short lifetime), and the server validates it during the handshake — so the connection is authenticated at the transport layer, before any application data flows. Use mTLS for service-to-service communication inside a zero-trust network (every service authenticates every other service), for high-assurance partner integrations (a bank's API requiring a client certificate from the partner), for IoT device authentication (each device has a cert), and for internal admin interfaces (the admin CLI presents a cert to access management endpoints). Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, Consul) implement mTLS transparently via sidecar proxies — every internal call is automatically mTLS without the application code being aware, with certificates rotating every 24 hours.

**Visual:**
```
one-way TLS (public HTTPS):
  client --[validates server cert]--> server
  client auth: cookie/token at app layer (after TLS)

mTLS (service mesh):
  svcA --[presents cert]--> [validates each other's cert] --> svcB
  transport-layer auth: no app-layer token needed
  certs from mesh CA, 24h lifetime, auto-rotate via sidecar
```

### Q5. How does certificate transparency (CT) improve the CA system?
**Answer:** Certificate transparency (RFC 9162) is a public, append-only log of every certificate issued by participating CAs. When a CA issues a certificate, it must submit the certificate (or a "pre-certificate") to at least two CT logs, which return signed timestamps (SCTs) that the server includes in its TLS handshake. Browsers refuse to trust certificates without SCTs, which forces CAs to log everything. The benefit is detection: a domain owner can monitor the CT logs for their domains and detect if a CA issued a certificate for their domain without authorization (a mis-issuance or a compromise) — historically, this happened repeatedly (DigiNotar 2011, Comodo 2011, Symantec 2017) and went undetected for months. With CT, Google detected Symantec's mis-issuance in days, leading to Symantec's eventual distrust. CT does not prevent mis-issuance, but it makes it visible, which is a major improvement over the previous "trust the CA blindly" model. The logs are publicly queryable (crt.sh, Google's CT log search), so anyone can see every certificate ever issued for any domain. The next evolution is to require CT for internal certificates and to add revocation checking that actually works (OCSP stapling + must-staple).

**Visual:**
```
CA issues cert -> submits to 2+ CT logs -> gets SCTs
server presents: cert + SCTs (in handshake)
browser: refuses trust without SCTs
domain owner: monitors crt.sh for their domains
  -> detects mis-issuance in days, not months
```

### Q6. Why is OCSP stapling necessary, and how does it work?
**Answer:** OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) lets a client check whether a certificate has been revoked — but the naive version (the client contacts the CA's OCSP responder on every connection) is slow (adds an extra round-trip), leaky (the CA learns every site the client visits), and brittle (if the OCSP responder is down, the client must choose between failing closed (block the site) or failing open (accept a possibly-revoked cert, which browsers do, defeating the purpose)). OCSP stapling solves this by having the server fetch the OCSP response from the CA periodically (e.g., daily) and "staple" it to its TLS handshake — the client verifies the CA-signed OCSP response without any extra round-trip and without leaking to the CA. The server must refresh the stapled response before it expires (typically 2-4 days). For higher assurance, "must-staple" certificates (an extension in the cert) require the client to reject the connection if no fresh OCSP response is stapled — this closes the fail-open loophole. Production servers should enable OCSP stapling; without it, revocation is effectively broken because browsers fail open. Cloudflare, Google, and large CDNs all staple OCSP responses.

**Visual:**
```
naive OCSP:
  client -> CA's OCSP responder: "is cert X revoked?"
  -> slow (extra RTT), leaky (CA sees client's destinations), brittle

OCSP stapling:
  server -> CA: fetch OCSP response daily (signed)
  client -> server: handshake
  server -> client: cert + stapled OCSP response (CA-signed)
  client: verify OCSP sig (no extra RTT, no leak)
  must-staple: client rejects if no fresh OCSP -> fail closed
```

### Q7. How does TLS 1.3 0-RTT work, and what are its security caveats?
**Answer:** 0-RTT (zero round-trip time) resumption lets a client that has previously connected to a server send application data in its very first flight, before the server has responded. It works by the server giving the client a session ticket (a pre-shared key, PSK, encrypted to a server-only key) at the end of the first connection; on the next connection, the client uses the PSK to encrypt application data immediately, and the server can decrypt it without a round-trip. The performance win is significant for latency-sensitive applications (a returning client can send an HTTP request in 0 RTT instead of 1 RTT). The security caveats are notable: 0-RTT data is replayable, because the server cannot distinguish a genuine 0-RTT request from a replayed one (the attacker recorded the first flight and resends it). This means 0-RTT must never be used for non-idempotent requests (a `POST /charges` would be double-charged on replay). Browsers and HTTP libraries restrict 0-RTT to safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) by default. Servers can implement anti-replay (track recently-seen PSK identifiers and reject duplicates) but this is complex in distributed systems. The guidance: enable 0-RTT for read-only traffic where the latency win matters, disable it for write traffic, and document the assumption clearly.

**Visual:**
```
first connection:
  client --[ClientHello + key_share]--> server  (1 RTT handshake)
  client <== session ticket (PSK) ===> server
  (full handshake, forward secrecy)

resumption (0-RTT):
  client --[ClientHello + PSK + 0-RTT data]--> server
  server: decrypts 0-RTT data with PSK, processes immediately
  (no round-trip before first data)

caveat: 0-RTT data is REPLAYABLE
  attacker records first flight, resends it
  -> server cannot distinguish replay
  -> never use for POST /charges, only for safe GETs
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your company's HTTPS certificate expired last night and the site is down. Walk me through your response and prevention.
**Answer:** Immediate response: identify the expired certificate (which domain, which LB or ingress), renew it via your ACME client (cert-manager, AWS ACM, or manually via the CA's dashboard), install the new certificate on the affected endpoints, and verify with `curl -v` or a browser that the new cert is being served. If renewal is delayed (CA outage, validation failure), obtain an emergency certificate from a backup CA or use a Cloudflare-fronted endpoint as a stopgap. Communicate to customers via status page. Prevention is the real fix: deploy automated certificate management so this never happens again. In Kubernetes, install cert-manager with a Let's Encrypt ClusterIssuer and configure it to renew certificates 30 days before expiry — it handles the entire lifecycle automatically. In AWS, use AWS Certificate Manager which auto-renews certificates it issues. Set up monitoring: Prometheus alerts on certificate expiry (with warnings at 30 days and critical at 7 days), and Synthetic checks that verify HTTPS endpoints daily. Run game days where you deliberately expire a cert in staging to verify the alerting and renewal pipeline. The deeper cultural fix: certificates are infrastructure, not paperwork — they must be managed by automation, not by a human with a calendar reminder.

**Visual:**
```
IMMEDIATE:
  1. identify expired cert (domain, LB)
  2. renew via ACME client (cert-manager, ACM, manual)
  3. install new cert, verify with curl -v
  4. communicate via status page
PREVENTION:
  - cert-manager + Let's Encrypt (auto-renew at 30d before expiry)
  - ACM (auto-renew for AWS-issued certs)
  - Prometheus alert: cert_expiry < 30d = warn, < 7d = critical
  - game day: deliberately expire staging cert
```

### Q2. You need to call a partner's API that requires a client certificate (mTLS). How do you set this up?
**Answer:** First, obtain a client certificate from the partner (they typically issue one per integration or require you to send a CSR for them to sign with their internal CA). Store the certificate and its private key in a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, Kubernetes secret with encryption at rest) — never in source control, never in a CI log. Configure your HTTP client to present the certificate on the TLS handshake: in Python `requests`, pass `cert=('client.crt', 'client.key')`; in Go, load the cert into a `tls.Config` with `Certificates`; in curl, `--cert client.crt --key client.key`. If the partner rotates the certificate periodically (common: 90-day lifetime), automate the renewal — fetch the new cert from the partner's API or via a CSR, store it in the secret manager, and reload it into your HTTP client without a service restart (Go's `tls.Config.GetClientCertificate` and Python's `HTTPAdapter` support dynamic cert loading). Monitor the certificate's expiry and alert 30 days before. Audit every call: log the certificate's serial number and the partner's endpoint, so you can attribute traffic. Finally, verify the partner's server certificate as well (mTLS is mutual) — pin to their CA or rely on the system trust store.

**Visual:**
```
partner CA -> issues client cert (90d) -> secret manager -> app
app -> partner API: TLS handshake
  client presents: client.crt (signed by partner CA)
  partner validates: client cert chain to partner CA
  partner presents: server cert
  app validates: server cert chain to system trust store
  -> mTLS established, app sends API request
renewal: every 60d, fetch new cert, store, reload (no restart)
```

### Q3. You are designing a microservices architecture. Should every internal call use mTLS?
**Answer:** Yes, in a zero-trust model. The traditional "soft" approach was: trust the internal network, encrypt only at the edge, leave internal calls as plaintext HTTP. This breaks down when (a) an attacker breaches one service and pivots internally, (b) an insider with network access snoops, (c) compliance requires encryption everywhere (PCI-DSS, HIPAA). The zero-trust model says: never trust the network, authenticate every call. mTLS is the standard implementation. The operational question is how to deploy it without overwhelming the application teams. The answer is a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect, AWS App Mesh): sidecar proxies handle mTLS transparently, the application makes a plaintext call to localhost, the sidecar wraps it in mTLS to the destination sidecar, which unwraps and forwards to the destination application. Certificates are issued by the mesh's CA, rotate every 24 hours, and are SPIFFE-identified for fine-grained authorization. The cost is: sidecar resource overhead (~10-50 MB RAM per pod), a small latency addition (~1 ms per hop), and the operational complexity of running the mesh's control plane. The benefit is: every internal call is authenticated and encrypted, revocation is automatic (certs expire in 24h), and the application code is unchanged. For greenfield microservices, adopt a mesh from day one.

**Visual:**
```
without mesh (plaintext internal):
  svcA --[plaintext HTTP]--> svcB   (anyone on the network can sniff/spoof)

with service mesh (mTLS, transparent):
  svcA -> sidecarA --[mTLS]--> sidecarB -> svcB
  sidecars: cert from mesh CA, 24h lifetime, auto-rotate
  svcA and svcB code: unchanged (plain HTTP to localhost)
```

### Q4. Your application talks to a database over TLS, but performance is critical. Should you encrypt the DB connection?
**Answer:** Yes, almost always. The performance overhead of TLS to a database is small (the connection is long-lived, so the handshake cost is amortized; AES-GCM with AES-NI is ~1-3% CPU overhead for the data), and the security gain is significant. Without TLS, anyone with network access between your application and the database (a compromised switch, a sniffer on the same VLAN, an insider running tcpdump) can read every query and result — including credentials, PII, payment data. With TLS, the connection is encrypted and the database can optionally authenticate the client via a client certificate (mTLS to the DB), which is stronger than a password. The main trade-off is operational: you must manage certificates for the database (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB all support TLS but require configuration), and connection pooling must handle TLS correctly (reuse the TLS session, not just the TCP connection). For very high-throughput workloads where the 1-3% matters, you can terminate TLS at a sidecar or use a connection pooler (PgBouncer, ProxySQL) that handles TLS to the DB and accepts plaintext from the application over localhost — the network segment between the app and the pooler is localhost (trusted), and the network segment between the pooler and the DB is encrypted. The default for new deployments should be TLS to the DB, with the rare exception justified explicitly.

**Visual:**
```
app --[TLS]--> DB
  handshake: amortized over long-lived connection
  data: AES-GCM, ~1-3% CPU with AES-NI
  gain: no plaintext query/result on the network
  + mTLS option: DB validates client cert (stronger than password)

high-throughput variant:
  app --[localhost plaintext]--> PgBouncer --[TLS]--> DB
  (pooler handles TLS, app trusts localhost)
```

### Q5. Your CDN offers "TLS termination at edge" with plaintext from CDN to origin. Is this safe?
**Answer:** It depends on what network the CDN-to-origin traffic crosses. If the origin is in the same VPC as the CDN's edge node (or on a dedicated private link like AWS CloudFront-Origins-Access-Control or Cloudflare Argo Tunnel), plaintext over that segment is acceptable — the traffic never crosses the public internet. If the origin is on the public internet (a routable IP), plaintext from CDN to origin is a serious vulnerability: anyone on the path between the CDN and the origin can read and modify the traffic, defeating the purpose of the edge TLS. The fix is "full TLS" or "origin TLS": configure the CDN to establish a second TLS connection to the origin, so the traffic is encrypted end-to-end (client → CDN is TLS, CDN → origin is also TLS). Cloudflare calls this "Full (strict)" mode and additionally validates the origin's certificate against a trusted CA or Cloudflare's origin CA. AWS CloudFront supports HTTPS to the origin and can require a valid cert. The cost is one extra TLS handshake per request at the CDN edge, which is negligible. The security gain is that the entire path is encrypted. The rare exception where plaintext CDN-to-origin is acceptable is when the origin is behind a private link and the data is non-sensitive — but the default should be full TLS.

**Visual:**
```
UNSAFE (origin on public internet):
  client --[TLS]--> CDN edge --[PLAINTEXT]--> origin (public IP)
  -> anyone on the path CDN->origin can read traffic

SAFE (full TLS, "Full (strict)"):
  client --[TLS]--> CDN edge --[TLS]--> origin
  -> end-to-end encrypted, CDN validates origin cert

ACCEPTABLE (rare):
  client --[TLS]--> CDN edge --[plaintext over private link]--> origin
  -> traffic never crosses public internet
```

### Q6. You suspect a man-in-the-middle attack on your mobile app's API calls. How do you detect and prevent it?
**Answer:** Detection: instrument the app to log the certificate chain it receives on each TLS handshake and report any unexpected certificate (e.g., the chain does not end at a trusted root, or the issuing CA changed unexpectedly). A sudden spike in unexpected certificates, especially from a small set of IPs or ASNs, indicates a MITM attempt (often a corporate proxy, a parental control app, or an actual attacker). Some apps pin their expected certificate or public key (certificate pinning / public key pinning) and refuse to connect if the presented cert does not match — this defeats MITM even if the attacker has a valid CA-issued cert (which happens when a CA is compromised or coerced). Prevention: implement certificate pinning for the most sensitive endpoints (login, payment), using the SPKI (Subject Public Key Info) hash rather than the full cert so that rotation does not break the pin. Have multiple pins (current + backup) so you can rotate. Ship pins via remote configuration (Firebase Remote Config, a settings endpoint) so you can update them without an app release — but be careful that the config endpoint itself is not pinned (chicken-and-egg). The trade-off: pinning breaks corporate proxies and SSL inspection, which some users need, so make it optional or scoped to sensitive endpoints. Also use HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) so the browser/app never falls back to plaintext HTTP. Modern mobile platforms (Android Network Security Config, iOS App Transport Security) provide native pinning support.

**Visual:**
```
detection:
  app logs cert chain on every TLS handshake
  unexpected CA or self-signed -> flag (possible MITM)

prevention (pinning):
  app has SPKI hash of expected cert
  on handshake: compare presented cert's SPKI to expected
  mismatch -> refuse connection (even if cert is "valid")
  multiple pins (current + backup) -> rotation works

trade-off:
  pinning breaks corporate proxies / SSL inspection
  -> scope to sensitive endpoints (login, payment), not all
```

### Q7. Your security team wants to inspect all TLS traffic for threats (a corporate TLS-interception proxy). What are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** TLS interception (also called SSL inspection or a corporate TLS proxy) means the corporate network intercepts all TLS traffic, presents a certificate signed by a corporate root CA (installed on all employee devices) to the client, and establishes a separate TLS connection to the destination server — decrypting, inspecting, and re-encrypting the traffic in the middle. The benefit is that the corporate security team can detect malware, exfiltration, and policy violations inside encrypted traffic, which otherwise looks opaque. The trade-offs are significant: (a) privacy — employees' browsing, banking, and personal accounts are decrypted and visible to the security team, raising legal and ethical issues (most deployments exempt financial and healthcare sites); (b) security — the corporate root CA is now a high-value target, and if compromised, an attacker can impersonate any site to all corporate devices (this has happened); (c) compatibility — many apps (banking, mobile, certificate-pinned apps) refuse the corporate cert and break; (d) performance — the proxy adds latency and is a bottleneck; (e) loss of forward secrecy — the proxy records the decrypted traffic, so forward secrecy is defeated for the corporate traffic segment. The modern approach is selective interception: intercept only unknown or risky traffic, exempt trusted financial and healthcare sites, and use endpoint-based detection (EDR) instead of network interception where possible. Treat the corporate root CA as the highest-value secret in the company.

**Visual:**
```
client --[TLS, corp CA cert]--> proxy --[TLS, real cert]--> server
  proxy decrypts, inspects, re-encrypts
  client trusts corp CA (installed on device)

benefits:
  + detect malware/exfil in encrypted traffic
  + enforce DLP policies

trade-offs:
  - privacy (banking, health visible to security team)
  - corp root CA = high-value target (compromise = impersonate any site)
  - breaks pinned apps (banking, mobile)
  - defeats forward secrecy (proxy records plaintext)
  - latency + bottleneck

modern: selective interception + EDR (endpoint detection) preferred
```
